content: Swine influenza, also known as swine flu, is a respiratory disease in pigs caused by influenza A viruses. It is not classified as a notifiable disease to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Swine influenza viruses (SIVs) that exhibit H1 or H3 hemagglutinin (HA) subtypes—specifically A(H1N1), A(H1N2), and A(H3N2)—are enzootic in pig populations globally. The last detection of an A(H2) virus in pigs occurred in 2006 in the United States. Due to the significant genetic diversity of SIVs, various lineages and clades have been identified based on their phylogenetic characteristics. SIVs circulating in North America and Europe are genetically distinct, while those found in Asia often contain genetic material originating from both regions. When introduced into pig herds, SIVs can cause high morbidity, although mortality is typically low. Recovery from infection generally occurs within 7 to 10 days. Clinical signs in pigs are usually mild and include fever, depression, coughing, nasal or ocular discharge, sneezing, breathing difficulties, eye redness or inflammation, and changes in appetite. Some SIVs may circulate silently within herds, causing asymptomatic or subclinical infections. While mortality is low, high morbidity can result in production losses due to delayed weight gain or abortion in affected pigs. Pigs are often referred to as mixing vessels because they are susceptible to both avian and human influenza viruses. This susceptibility allows for genetic reassortment between influenza viruses from different species, potentially leading to the emergence of viruses with zoonotic or pandemic potential. Beyond pigs, SIVs have also been detected in humans and various bird species. Animal influenza viruses, particularly avian and swine influenza viruses, can occasionally infect humans, resulting in zoonotic infections. Zoonotic diseases are those transmitted from animals to humans, while reverse zoonosis refers to transmission from humans to animals. Current zoonotic influenza viruses have not demonstrated sustained human-to-human transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) regularly assesses the risk posed by zoonotic influenza viruses to human health, including the potential for sustained human-to-human transmission. Avian influenza viruses, such as A(H5N1), A(H7N9), and A(H9N2), have sporadically caused disease in humans following infection. Human infection can occur through direct contact with infected birds or their by-products (e.g., during handling, culling, slaughtering, or processing) or indirect contact with environments contaminated by bodily fluids from infected birds. Rarely, human cases of avian influenza infection have been reported following contact with an intermediate species. Exposure to avian influenza viruses can lead to a range of symptoms in humans, from conjunctivitis or mild flu-like symptoms to severe acute respiratory disease and, in some cases, death. The severity of the disease depends on the specific virus and the characteristics of the infected individual. Rarely, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms have also been reported. To date, only subtypes of H3, H5, H6, H7, H9, and H10 avian influenza viruses are known to have caused human infections. Serological studies suggest that some undetected human infections may occur in occupationally exposed groups. Human cases of infection with SIVs have also been reported. When an SIV infects a human, it is classified as a variant (v) virus, such as H1N1v, H1N2v, or H3N2v. Close proximity to infected pigs or visiting locations where pigs are kept has been identified as a factor in most human cases. Preventing and controlling influenza in animals is essential to minimize the circulation of animal influenza viruses, thereby reducing the risk of zoonotic human infections and disease. These measures should be developed and implemented in an integrated manner, with collaboration between public health and animal health sectors at both administrative and technical levels, applying a One Health approach. Local FAO offices can provide more information on prevention measures being implemented in the animal sector. Efforts to reduce human exposure to animal influenza viruses and prevent human disease should focus on the interface between humans, animals, and the environment. Preventive measures should target occupational risk groups, such as veterinarians, farmers, farmworkers in contact with poultry, swine, or mink, and backyard bird and pig keepers, as well as individuals in contact with potentially infected animals, such as live animal market workers, slaughterhouse workers, meat processors, or households practicing home slaughtering of animals. Surveillance to detect possible human cases should be intensified, and protocols for rapid response to the first detection of a human case in an area should be in place and reviewed as needed. The animal health sector is responsible for preventing and controlling disease outbreaks in animals. Reporting new and ongoing influenza detections and outbreaks in animals is crucial for focusing human health activities in affected areas and raising awareness among professionals working with potentially infected animals, as well as the public. Sharing information on human cases with the animal health sector is equally important to ensure targeted response activities. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations promotes food security and good nutrition by providing access to knowledge, policy advice, and technical assistance to member countries. FAO publishes information and guidance on avian influenza and provides direct technical assistance to countries through its headquarters, regional and country offices, expert missions, capacity-building, and laboratory support. FAO also fosters collaboration, communication, and coordination between countries and regions. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) improves animal health and welfare worldwide by setting international standards for animal health and zoonosis prevention and response. WOAH collects and disseminates official animal disease information from its member countries and collaborates with national veterinary services and FAO to provide technical assistance, such as laboratory support, to countries. Preparedness activities should include developing, testing, and reviewing strategies for communication and infodemic management, identifying roles and responsibilities for implementation, and developing standard operating procedures (SOPs) and templates. Partnerships should be mapped and trust built among stakeholders, networks, and communities to lay the foundation for response activities.
